parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A ball of mass m strikes a vertical wall horizontally at speed u and rebounds in the opposite direction at speed v. The collision lasts time T. Determine the magnitude of the average force exerted by the wall.

answer.text: The momentum change has magnitude m(u + v), so the average force is m(u + v)/T.

duplicate-7400f9d92fda4cac.hint: Express one complete turn in radians and identify the time for that turn.
notes: Angular speed is ω = 2π/T; linear speed at radius r is v = ωr.
Convert the period to seconds before quoting rad s⁻¹. Angular speed and linear speed are different quantities.

ibd-b968d648a18e0de4-q8:whole.hint: Choose the object or system and identify the resultant force, rather than using one force on its own.
notes: Newton’s second law is ΣF = ma. Resolve into independent directions; zero acceleration requires zero resultant force in that direction.
Newton’s third-law forces act on different bodies and are the same kind of interaction. Balanced forces act on the same body.

ibd-d439dc8092aa4796-q6:whole.hint: Resolve forces parallel and perpendicular to the contact surface. Decide which way the object would tend to move.
notes: For a simple incline, weight has components mg sin θ down the plane and mg cos θ into it. Other applied forces can change the normal reaction.
Kinetic friction has magnitude μ_k N. Static friction adjusts up to μ_s N; use the maximum only at impending slip, and choose its direction to oppose relative slipping.

ibd-d439dc8092aa4796-q8:whole.hint: Choose a system containing the interacting objects and compare its total momentum before and after the event.
notes: When external impulse is negligible, Σmu = Σmv. Keep velocity signs, and apply the equation separately in each direction for a two-dimensional collision.
“Sticks together” gives one shared final velocity. Kinetic energy is conserved only for an elastic collision; momentum conservation alone does not make a collision elastic.

ibd-d439dc8092aa4796-q21:whole.hint: Draw a force equation for each connected body, using compatible positive directions along the string.
notes: An inextensible taut string links the accelerations. A light string over an ideal pulley has the same tension on both sides.
To find acceleration, combine the equations to eliminate internal tension. Then substitute back into a single-body equation to find the tension.

ibd-e859d9a6b4b57fcf-q5:whole.hint: Choose the object or system and identify the resultant force, rather than using one force on its own.
notes: Newton’s second law is ΣF = ma. Resolve into independent directions; zero acceleration requires zero resultant force in that direction.
Newton’s third-law forces act on different bodies and are the same kind of interaction. Balanced forces act on the same body.

ibd-e859d9a6b4b57fcf-q6:whole.hint: Consider the momentum carried away or brought in by the mass flowing each second.
notes: Force is the rate of momentum change. For a stream brought to rest, its magnitude is mass flow rate multiplied by the change in velocity.
For density ρ, area A and speed v, mass flow rate is ρAv. Include direction and any incoming momentum when applying the relation to a nozzle or rocket.

ibd-833a4564a23d92a7-q6:whole.hint: Check whether the graph shows total spring length or extension.
notes: Hooke’s law is F = kx within the proportional region, where x is extension beyond natural length.
On force against extension, gradient is k; on extension or length against force it is 1/k. A length intercept can reveal natural length.

duplicate-d3bbda69e618ff1f.hint: Think about the change in momentum during the contact. If you have a force–time graph, look at its area.
notes: Impulse is Δp = ∫F dt. For an average force, F_avg = Δp/Δt; a triangular pulse has half the impulse of a rectangle with the same height and width.
Include the direction of the initial and final velocities. A rebound can give a larger momentum change than simply stopping.

“Sticks together” gives one shared final velocity. Kinetic energy is conserved only for an elastic collision; momentum conservation alone does not make a collision elastic.
